slides: Let's continue with right triangles inside solids.

slides.say: The second idea is right triangles inside solids. Many 3D questions are solved with Pythagoras, once we find the right triangle.
Why are there right triangles? The height stands straight on the base, like a pole on a flat floor.
at: like a pole on a flat floor

slides.say: So the height makes a right angle with every line on the floor that starts at its foot. Not only with one of them, with all of them.
at: with every line on the floor

slides.say: Let's see it in a cone. The radius is five, and the slant height, the line along the outside, is thirteen. What's the height?
at: Let's see it in a cone

slides.say: The height, the radius and the slant height make a triangle. The radius lies on the base, so the angle between the height and the radius is a right angle.
Let's pull this triangle out. The slant height, thirteen, is the hypotenuse. The radius, five, is a leg.
So h squared plus five squared is thirteen squared. One hundred sixty-nine minus twenty-five is one hundred forty-four, so h is twelve. That's the triple five, twelve, thirteen.
at: So h squared plus five squared

slides.say: Now a pyramid with a square base. The side of the base is eight, and each slanted edge is nine. What's the height?
at: Now a pyramid with a square base

slides.say: The height comes down to the middle of the square, where the diagonals meet.
So we have a triangle. The height, half of a diagonal, and a slanted edge. The angle at the middle is a right angle, because half the diagonal lies on the base.
Remember the silver triangle. The diagonal of a square is the side times root two. So the diagonal is eight root two, and half of it is four root two.
at: the diagonal is eight root two

slides.say: Now let's pull the triangle out. The edge, nine, is the hypotenuse. The square of four root two is sixteen times two, thirty-two.
So h squared is eighty-one minus thirty-two, forty-nine. And h is seven.
Now a cube with edge four. A diagonal on a face is like the diagonal of a square, the edge times root two. So it's four root two.
at: Now a cube with edge four

slides.say: Now the diagonal through the inside of the cube, the body diagonal. Look at this triangle. The vertical edge stands on the bottom face, so it makes a right angle with the face diagonal.
Let's pull it out. The legs are four and four root two. Four squared is sixteen, and the square of four root two is thirty-two. Together, forty-eight.
Root forty-eight is root sixteen times root three, four root three. So the body diagonal is four root three.

This is true in every cube. The face diagonal is the edge times root two. The body diagonal is the edge times root three. Why root three? Edge squared, plus two edges squared, makes three edges squared.
at: The face diagonal is the edge times
The body diagonal is the edge times

slides.say: So a cube with edge five has a face diagonal of five root two, and a body diagonal of five root three.
In a box, the edges are not equal, so there's no fixed ratio. We use the same two right triangles. Here's a box, two by three, with height six.
First the diagonal of the base. Its square is two squared plus three squared, four plus nine, thirteen. We don't even need its root.
at: First the diagonal of the base

slides.say: Then the second triangle, with the height. Thirteen plus six squared is thirteen plus thirty-six, forty-nine. So the body diagonal is root forty-nine, seven.
Or in one step, the square root of the three edges squared. Two squared plus three squared plus six squared is forty-nine, and its root is seven. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
